one_liner: SIMD two-choice quotient-style filter with deletes; about 2x faster inserts than the Morton filter and steady throughput to 90% load.
what_it_does: An approximate-membership filter (insert, query, delete) from the SIGMOD 2021 paper by Pandey, Conway, Durie, Bender, Farach-Colton and Johnson. The whole API is vqf_init(nslots) plus three calls, vqf_insert, vqf_is_present and vqf_remove, and each takes a 64-bit hash that the caller computes. The library does not hash keys, and it has no destroy, resize, count, merge, iterate or serialize operations. It is not a drop-in replacement for the Morton or cuckoo filter C++ classes: you vendor the sources and hash your own keys.
how_it_is_fast: Each 64-byte block holds 48 8-bit fingerprints plus a 128-bit metadata bitvector that unary-encodes run boundaries for 80 buckets. That is quotient-filter/Robin Hood layout confined to one block (the paper's 'mini-filter'). A lookup broadcasts the fingerprint, compares it against the whole block in one AVX-512 compare (two AVX2 compares on the fallback path), and masks the hits to the bucket's run using BMI2 pdep/tzcnt rank-select on the metadata; power-of-two-choices hashing means it checks two blocks. An insert picks the less-loaded of the two blocks, looking at the alternate only once the primary is about 75% full, then shifts tags with one vpermb permute from precomputed shuffle tables and updates the metadata with pdep. There are no cuckoo kick-out chains, so insert cost stays nearly flat as the filter fills.
when_to_use: Dynamic filters (inserts plus deletes) filled to high load: in the authors' 2^28-slot data, VQF inserts run at about 22 Mops up to 60% load and about 17 Mops at 90%, while the cuckoo filter falls from 33 Mops to about 2 Mops.

Insert-heavy ingest on x86-64 servers with AVX-512 (the 8-bit fast path needs VBMI) and hardware-speed BMI2 (Intel Haswell or later, AMD Zen 3 or later), where a roughly 0.44% false-positive rate (8-bit tags) or roughly 0.002% (16-bit tags) is acceptable.
Multi-threaded, insert-only build phases: the THREAD=1 build uses per-block spinlocks, and the authors' TXN data shows 62.3 ns/insert on 1 thread vs 18.4 ns on 4 threads.
Keys you can already reduce to a well-mixed 64-bit hash, such as k-mers or IDs, with sizes from about 2^21 to 2^30 slots (the range the authors and later papers benchmarked).
A reference or baseline implementation when evaluating quotient- or pocket-dictionary-style filters.
when_not_to_use: Lookup-dominated workloads: in the authors' own data the cuckoo filter answers lookups faster (25-31 ns vs 34 ns at 2^28). Schmitz et al. 2025 measured 25.4 M lookups/s for VQF vs 32-44 M/s for their cuckoo variants and 39 M/s for the Prefix filter.
Insert-only or static sets: the Prefix filter builds 1.39-1.46x faster at similar space, and xor or binary fuse filters are smaller and faster for static sets.
Non-x86 targets (ARM, Apple Silicon), MSVC or clang-only toolchains, and AMD Zen 1/Zen 2, where PDEP/PEXT are microcoded at about 18-cycle latency.
You need a tunable FPR, counting, resizing, merging, serialization or enumeration. Only 8- or 16-bit tags exist, fixed at compile time; the CQF covers the rest.

Production use needing maturity: no tests, releases or library target, and the May 2024 commit rewrote bucket and alternate-bucket hashing after the paper's measurements, with no published re-benchmark from the authors.

integration.dependencies: vqf_filter.c needs only libc and x86 intrinsics headers. libssl/libcrypto (RAND_bytes), pthread and libitm are linked by the Makefile for the bundled benchmark drivers.
integration.min_toolchain: GCC/g++ with -std=c++11: vqf_filter.c is C++ despite its .c extension (reinterpret_cast, references, <algorithm>). The Makefile hard-codes gcc/g++ with -fgnu-tm and -march=native.
integration.platforms: x86-64 only; BMI2 (pdep/pext/tzcnt) and at least AVX2 are required. The fast 8-bit path needs AVX-512 VBMI. The Makefile detects AVX-512 with Linux lscpu.
integration.thread_safety: Not thread-safe by default. With -DENABLE_THREADS (make THREAD=1), only vqf_insert takes per-block spinlocks. vqf_is_present and vqf_remove are unsynchronized, so queries or deletes running alongside inserts are unsafe. PR #1, which added those locks, was closed unmerged.

gotchas: The caller supplies the hash. Bucket = hash % range and tag = bits 32-39 (tag 0 is remapped to 1), so a poorly mixed 64-bit hash raises the FPR. Duplicate inserts consume extra slots, and removing a key that was never inserted can delete another key's fingerprint.

The AVX-512 path is guarded by __AVX512BW__, and the Makefile checks for avx512bw. The default 8-bit code, however, calls _mm512_permutexvar_epi8, which GCC places under avx512vbmi, so -march=native builds on BW-only CPUs (Skylake-SP, Cascade Lake) will likely fail to compile (inferred from the code, not tested). TAG_BITS is a hard #define in vqf_filter.h, so switching to 16-bit tags means editing the header.

Library hygiene: vqf_init prints 'Size: N' to stdout and checks malloc only with assert. There is no destroy function (call free()). A failed insert prints 'vqf filter is full.' to stderr and returns false. The 64-byte blocks start 48 bytes after the malloc'd header, so whether each block fits in one cache line depends on the allocator.

The full-block check in vqf_insert runs only inside the branch taken when the alternate bucket is in a different block. If both candidate buckets map to the same full block, the insert proceeds without a capacity check and can overwrite the last stored tag. This comes from code reading and was not tested.
pick_this_over_siblings_when: Pick VQF over the cuckoo filter (efficient/cuckoofilter) or the Morton filter when you need deletes and insert throughput that holds at 80-90% load, and over the Prefix Filter when you need deletions or an AVX2 fallback (the Prefix Filter is insert-only and needs AVX-512). Choose the CQF instead for counting, resizing or merging, the cuckoo filter for lookup-bound workloads, and xor/binary fuse filters for static sets.
verified_claims_summary: The authors' raw data in the repo (scripts/Performance.gnumeric: 2^28 slots, 8-bit tags, CPU and compiler not recorded, pre-2024 hashing code) backs the paper's claims: 40.1 ns vs 80.1 ns per insert against the Morton filter (2.0x), and 3.4x insert scaling from 1 to 4 threads; it also shows lookups at 34.3 ns vs 25-31 ns for the cuckoo filter, so VQF is slower on lookups rather than at parity. An independent run of the current code (Schmitz et al. 2025, AMD Ryzen 9 9950X, 2^30 slots) measured 22.1 M inserts/s and 25.4 M lookups/s, behind the Prefix filter (33.2 / 39.1) on both; the paper PDF itself returned 403, so its setup is unverified.
status_note: Stale: the last commit (2024-05-19) rewrote the hashing, and the repo has 0 open issues and 13 stars. It is BSD-3-Clause and small (vqf_filter.c is about 630 lines), so it is easy to vendor, but it ships no library target, tests or releases.
